intro: Modal particles (Modalpartikeln) such as doch, ja, denn, mal, halt, eben, eigentlich, wohl, schon, ruhig, bloß, nur and etwa do not change what a sentence says but how the speaker feels about it: impatience, reproach, reassurance, resignation, surprise. They are unstressed, stand in the middle field (usually after the finite verb and pronouns), cannot open a sentence and have no single English translation; English uses tone, tags or words like just, really, surely, after all. Which particles are possible depends on the sentence type: denn and eigentlich live in questions, mal and doch soften or urge in requests, ja and doch point to shared knowledge in statements, bloß and nur carry wishes and warnings, etwa marks an incredulous yes/no question. One particle is special: stressed JA in a command (Fass das JA nicht an!) turns it into a warning. Understanding them in interviews and conversations, and using a few naturally yourself, is what makes your German sound like people really talk.
tips[0].title: Statements: ja, doch, eben, halt, wohl, schon
tips[0].text: ja = as we both know; doch = you should know / contrary to what you think; eben / halt = that is simply how it is; wohl = I suppose; schon = it will be all right.
tips[0].check.why: In a statement schon reassures: it will be all right. denn and etwa belong in questions.
tips[1].title: Questions: denn, eigentlich, etwa, bloß/nur
tips[1].text: denn makes a question involved or impatient; eigentlich shifts to a new topic; etwa in a yes/no question expects or hopes for no; bloß/nur in a w-question expresses alarm.
tips[1].trap: etwa in a question is not approximately: Hast du etwa gelogen? = You didn’t lie, did you? The answer expected is no.
tips[1].check.why: denn makes a question sound involved and concerned; ja and halt are statement particles.
tips[2].title: Requests and warnings: mal, doch, ruhig, JA, bloß
tips[2].text: mal softens (just); doch urges in a friendly way (why don’t you); ruhig gives reassuring permission (feel free); stressed JA, bloß and nur make a warning urgent.
tips[2].check.why: ruhig in a request gives reassuring permission: go ahead, feel free.
tips[3].title: Wishes: doch, bloß, nur
tips[3].text: Unreal wishes with Konjunktiv II need one of these particles; without it the sentence sounds unfinished.
tips[3].check.why: A stand-alone wish in the Konjunktiv II needs nur, bloß or doch to sound like a wish.
table.caption: Modal particles by sentence type
remember[0]: Particles are unstressed and never stand at the start of a sentence (exception: warning JA is stressed).
remember[1]: Questions: denn, eigentlich, etwa; requests: mal, doch, ruhig; statements: ja, doch, halt, eben, wohl, schon.
remember[2]: Several can combine in a fixed order: ja doch, doch mal, denn eigentlich.
mistakes[0].why: Modal particles stand in the middle field, after the verb, never in first position.
mistakes[1].why: In a yes/no question etwa is read as the particle of incredulity; use ungefähr for approximately.
mistakes[2].why: ja is a statement particle; questions take denn or eigentlich.
mistakes[3].why: A stand-alone wish needs a particle to be heard as a wish.
hook: Little words like doch, ja, denn and halt carry the mood of a sentence; use them and your German sounds like real conversation.
recall.known: From the earlier particle lessons: denn, doch, ja, mal, halt, eben, schon.
recall.today: Sorting them by sentence type: statements, questions, requests and wishes.
